answer:
**Hypothesis (answer).** All 18 of 18 Experimental Economics originals in this dataset — i.e., **100% (18/18)** on the primary "in-person in the original experiment" reading (project=='ee' AND online.o==0, deduped by id; numerator = 18, denominator = 18, n = 18) — were conducted in a lab setting. Under alternative defensible operationalizations of "lab setting," the proportion is essentially identical: 18/18 (100%) for in-person + subject pool in {students, community}; 18/18 (100%) for in-person + cash/mixed compensation; 18/18 (100%) for original-and-replication-both-in-person (same_online==1); and 17/18 (≈ 94.4%) under the strict "in-person AND students-only" reading — the gap is entirely driven by one row (Charness & Dufwenberg 2011, "Participation") whose subject pool is labelled "community" rather than "students", although it was clearly run in person. The replication side (online.r) is identical to the original side in this dataset: online.r==0 and same_online==1 for all 18 rows, so the proportion is unchanged whether you count originals or replications.

**Sensitivity range:** 94.44% – 100.00% (17/18 – 18/18) across S1–S5.

**Workflow.** Loaded data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 × 57) and selected `project=='ee'` (n=18); deduped by `id` (defensive — values were already unique). Defined "lab" as `online.o == 0` on the originals to compute the primary proportion. Computed five sensitivity checks S1–S5 on the same 18 rows. Cross-confirmed the 18 ee originals against data/meta-regression_replication_success_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (which has 18 "Experimental Economics" rows but no lab/setting columns) by surname-set equality — intersection = 18/18, no symmetric difference. Saved numbers to artifacts/results.json; the executed script is artifacts/analysis.py.

**Caveats.** (i) n = 18 is the entirety of the Experimental Economics replication-project subset in this dataset; it is not a population claim about all Experimental Economics studies. (ii) CSV2 carries no setting information and contributes nothing to the proportion (used only as a cross-reference). (iii) `online.o`, `online.r`, `subjects.o`, `compensation.o`, and `same_online` are fully observed for ee (no NaN), so no imputation was needed. (iv) `lab_id` is NaN for all 18 ee rows (it indexes replication labs in the multi-lab projects, not the original-study setting here), so it is not part of the denominator.

payload.hypothesis: Among the 18 Experimental Economics originals in the supplied meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (project=='ee', deduped by id), all 18 were conducted in a lab setting under the in-person operationalization (online.o == 0): 18/18 = 100.00%. Sensitivity range across alternative operationalizations is 94.44%–100.00% (17/18 under the strict students-only reading vs. 18/18 under in-person-only, in-person + subject pool ∈ {students, community}, in-person + compensation ∈ {cash, mixed}, and original-and-replication-both-in-person). The single row responsible for the S1↔S2 discrepancy is Charness & Dufwenberg (AER 2011) "Participation", whose subject pool is labelled "community" but whose experiment was clearly in-person.
